content.paragraph: Recall from Section 11.1 that Zeno, in one of his paradoxes, observed that in order for a man standing in a room to walk to a wall, he would first have to walk half the distance to the wall, then half the remaining distance ($$\frac{1}{4}$$ of the total), and then again half of what still remains $$\left( \frac{1}{8} \right)$$ , and so on (see Figure 1). Because this process can always be continued, Zeno argued that the man can never reach the wall.

note.title: Theorem
note.paragraph: If the series $$\sum\limits_{n = 1}^{\infty}a_{n}$$ is convergent, then $$\underset{n\rightarrow\infty}{\lim}a_{n} = 0$$ .

note.title: Proof
note.paragraph: Let $$s_{n} = a_{1} + a_{2} + \cdots + a_{n}$$ . Then $$a_{n} = s_{n} - s_{n - 1}$$ . Since $$\sum a_{n}$$ is convergent, the sequence $$\left\{ s_{n} \right\}$$ is convergent. Let $$\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}s_{n} = s$$ . Since $$\left. n - 1\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ as $$\left. n\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ , we also have $$\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}s_{n - 1} = s$$ . Therefore

subsection.paragraph: Note With any series $$a_{n}$$ we associate two sequences: the sequence $$\left\{ s_{n} \right\}$$ of its partial sums and the sequence $$\left\{ a_{n} \right\}$$ of its terms. If $$\sum a_{n}$$ is convergent, then the limit of the sequence $$\left\{ s_{n} \right\}$$ is $$s$$ (the sum of the series) and, as Theorem 6 asserts, the limit of the sequence $$\left\{ a_{n} \right\}$$ is $$0$$ .

Warning The converse of Theorem 6 is not true in general. If $$\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}a_{n} = 0$$ , we cannot conclude that $$\sum a_{n}$$ is convergent. Observe that for the harmonic series $$\sum 1 \slash n$$ we have $$\left. a_{n} = 1 \slash n\rightarrow 0 \right.$$ as $$\left. n\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ , but we showed in Example 8 that $$1 \slash n$$ is divergent.

note.title: Test for Divergence
note.paragraph: If $$\lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}a_{n}$$ does not exist or if $$\lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}a_{n} \neq 0$$ , then the series $$\sum\limits_{n = 1}^{\infty}a_{n}$$ is divergent.

subsection.paragraph: The Test for Divergence follows from Theorem 6 because, if the series is not divergent, then it is convergent, and so $$\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}a_{n} = 0$$ .

If we find that $$\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}a_{n} = 0$$ , this fact tells us nothing about the convergence or divergence of $$\sum a_{n}$$ . item.paragraph: What is the difference between a sequence and a series?
A sequence is an ordered list of numbers whereas a series is the sum of a list of numbers.

The Cantor set, named after the German mathematician Georg Cantor (1845–1918), is constructed as follows. We start with the closed interval $$\left\lbrack {0,1} \right\rbrack$$ and remove the open interval $$\left( {\frac{1}{3},\frac{2}{3}} \right)$$ . That leaves the two intervals $$\left\lbrack {0,\frac{1}{3}} \right\rbrack$$ and $$\left\lbrack {\frac{2}{3},1} \right\rbrack$$ and we remove the open middle third of each. Four intervals remain and again we remove the open middle third of each of them. We continue this procedure indefinitely, at each step removing the open middle third of every interval that remains from the preceding step. The Cantor set consists of the numbers that remain in $$\left\lbrack {0,1} \right\rbrack$$ after all those intervals have been removed.

item.paragraph: Show that the total length of all the intervals that are removed is $$1$$ . Despite that, the Cantor set contains infinitely many numbers. Give examples of some numbers in the Cantor set.

Find $$\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}a_{n}$$ in terms of $$a_{1}$$ and $$a_{2}$$ by expressing $$a_{n + 1} - a_{n}$$ in terms of $$a_{2} - a_{1}$$ and summing a series.

statement.paragraph: Consider the series $$\sum_{n = 1}^{\infty}n \slash \left( {n + 1} \right)!$$ .

item.paragraph: Find the partial sums $$s_{1}$$ , $$s_{2}$$ , $$s_{3}$$ , and $$s_{4}$$ . Do you recognize the denominators? Use the pattern to guess a formula for $$s_{n}$$ .
Use mathematical induction to prove your guess.
Show that the given infinite series is convergent, and find its sum.

statement.paragraph: The figure shows infinitely many circles approaching the vertices of an equilateral triangle, each circle touching other circles and sides of the triangle. If the triangle has sides of length $$1$$ , find the total area occupied by the circles.

figure.alt_text: A triangle with a horizontal base has seven circles within it. The first circle is big and touches all three sides of the triangle. The second circle is much smaller than the first and is placed between the big circle and the two sides forming the bottom left vertex of the triangle. The third circle is much smaller than the second one and is drawn in such a way that it touches the second circle and the bottom and left side. Similarly, four circles are placed at the right and top vertices, two each, in the same fashion.
